title: ग, ज, ब, म, न, ल, स, य sound as in English
body: These letters are close to English g (as in “go”), j, b, m, n, l, s and y. न and ल are said with the tongue a little further forward, touching the teeth.

title: A consonant on its own carries a short “a”
body: A consonant with no vowel sign is read with a short “a”, like the “u” in “but”. The letter अ is the same sound at the start of a syllable. This “a” is often dropped (see the rules on the silent “a”).

title: The “a” at the end of a word is silent
body: A consonant at the end of a word, with no vowel sign, is said without its “a”: घर is “ghar”, not “gha-ra”. The one-letter word न (“not”) keeps it: “na”.

title: क, च, प have no puff of air
body: क, च and प are k, ch and p said without the puff of air English puts after them, like the k in “skin” or the p in “spin”. Hold a hand before your mouth: you should feel almost nothing.

title: आ and ा are a long “aa”
body: आ at the start of a syllable and the sign ा after a consonant are a long “aa”, as in “father”. Keep it long even when the syllable is not stressed.

title: Stress is light and goes to the heaviest syllable
body: Hindi stress is weak and never shortens a vowel. It goes to the heaviest syllable: a long vowel plus a consonant (TAAB) beats a long vowel or a closing consonant alone, which beats a short open syllable. If two tie, stress the one before the last syllable.

title: ए and े are “ay” without the glide
body: ए and the sign े are a long pure “e”, like “ay” in “say” but without sliding into “ee” at the end.

title: र is a quick tap of the tongue
body: र is a light tap of the tongue tip, like the “tt” in American “butter”, or a lightly rolled r. Always say it, also at the end of a word and before a consonant.

title: ई and ी are a long “ee”
body: ई and the sign ी are a long “ee”, as in “see”. Keep them clearly longer than ि.

title: त and द touch the teeth
body: त and द are a t and d with the tip of the tongue pressed against the back of the upper front teeth, softer than English t and d, as in Spanish or Italian. त has no puff of air.

title: ह is always said
body: ह is like English “h”, a little breathier. Say it everywhere, also between vowels and at the end of a word.

title: इ and ि are a short “i”
body: इ and the sign ि are a short “i”, as in “bit”. The sign ि is written before the consonant but said after it: दिन is d + i + n.

title: The “a” between two sounded vowels is dropped
body: When a consonant with no vowel sign sits between a vowel and a consonant that has a vowel sign, its “a” is usually skipped: कमरा is “kam-raa”, not “ka-ma-raa”.

title: A half letter or ् means no vowel
body: When a consonant has no vowel, it is written as a half letter joined to the next one (स्त in दोस्त), or with a small slanted stroke ् under it. Say the two consonants together.

title: ओ and ो are a pure “oh”
body: ओ and the sign ो are a long pure “o”, like “oh” but without sliding into “oo” at the end.

title: ं with no consonant after it makes the vowel nasal
body: Where no consonant follows, the dot ं means the vowel is said partly through the nose, as in French “bon”. It is used instead of ँ when a vowel sign sits above the line. The respellings write this as n.

title: उ and ु are a short “u” as in “put”
body: उ and the sign ु (under the consonant) are a short “u”, as in “put”, never as in “cut”.

title: ऐ and ै are like the “a” in “bad”
body: ऐ and the sign ै are a long open “e”, like the “a” in “bad”, stretched. Many speakers in eastern India say it more like “ai” in “aisle”.

title: ट and ड are said with the tongue curled back
body: For ट and ड, curl the tip of the tongue back and touch the roof of the mouth behind the gum ridge. They sound a bit like an American t and d, but harder. Keep them apart from त and द.

title: व is between “v” and “w”
body: व is a soft sound between English v and w: touch the upper teeth lightly to the lower lip. After a consonant (स्व, द्व) it is closer to “w”.

title: ख, छ, फ come with a strong puff of air
body: ख, छ and फ are k, ch and p followed by a strong puff of air, stronger than in English “kit”. ख is not the throaty “loch” sound (that is ख़). Many speakers say फ as “f”.

title: ं before a consonant is an “n” or “m”
body: The dot ं before a consonant is an n-sound made where the next consonant is: “m” before प, ब, म; “ng” before क, ग; “n” elsewhere.

title: थ and ध are never English “th”
body: थ and ध are the teeth sounds त and द followed by a puff of air or a breathy “h”, as in “at home” and “mad house” said quickly. They are never the “th” of “think” or “this”.

title: A short “a” before ह sounds like “e”
body: When ह has no vowel sign of its own, the short “a” before it sounds like the “e” in “bed”: कहना is “keh-naa”, यह is “yeh”. वह is usually said “voh”.

title: औ and ौ are like the “aw” in “law”
body: औ and the sign ौ are a long open “o”, like “aw” in “law”. Many speakers in eastern India say it more like “ow” in “cow”.

title: घ, झ, भ are a g, j, b with a breathy “h”
body: घ, झ and भ are g, j and b followed by a breathy “h”, as in “doghouse”, “hedgehog”, “clubhouse” said quickly as one sound.

title: श and ष are both “sh”
body: श and ष are both said “sh”, as in “shop”. ष comes in words from Sanskrit.

title: ऊ and ू are a long “oo”
body: ऊ and the sign ू are a long “oo”, as in “food”.

title: ँ makes the vowel nasal
body: The moon-and-dot ँ means the vowel is said partly through the nose, without a full n after it. The respellings write this as n.

title: फ़ is “f”
body: फ with a dot below (फ़) is an English “f”.

title: ड़ is a quick flap, close to “r”
body: ड़ (ड with a dot) is made by curling the tongue back and flicking it forward against the roof of the mouth. It sounds like a quick “r”. It never starts a word.

title: A small hook on top is an r said first
body: An r with no vowel before another consonant is written as a small hook (र्) on top of that consonant, or on top of its vowel sign. Say the r first: in कार्ड the hook sits on ड but the r comes before it.

title: A slanted stroke at the foot of a letter is an r after it
body: An r right after a consonant is a small slanted stroke at the foot of that consonant (प्र is “pr”). Under ट and ड it is a small “^” shape (ट्र, ड्र).

title: ज़ is “z”
body: ज with a dot below (ज़) is an English “z”, in words from Persian, Arabic and English. Some speakers say it as ज, and some texts leave out the dot.

title: A doubled consonant is held longer
body: A consonant written twice (च्च, ल्ल, म्म; च्छ is च + छ) is held for a moment before release, as in “book case” or “midday”. Making it short can change the word.

title: ठ and ढ are the curled-back sounds with breath
body: ठ and ढ are ट and ड (tongue curled back) followed by a puff of air or a breathy “h”.

title: ख़ is the throaty “kh” of “loch”
body: ख with a dot below (ख़) is a rough sound from the back of the throat, like Scottish “loch”. Many speakers say it as ख.

title: ऑ and ॉ are the “o” in “hot”
body: ऑ and the sign ॉ (a small moon over ा) are used in English words for the short “o” of British “hot”, “doctor”, “copy”.

title: ढ़ is the same flap with a breathy “h”
body: ढ़ (ढ with a dot) is the flap of ड़ followed by a breathy “h”, written here “rh”.

title: त्र and श्र are t + r and sh + r
body: त्र and श्र have their own shapes, but they are just त + र (“tr”, with the tongue on the teeth) and श + र (“shr”).

title: क़ is a “k” from deep in the throat
body: क with a dot below (क़) is a k made further back, where you swallow. Many speakers say it as an ordinary क.

title: ण is an n with the tongue curled back
body: ण is an n said with the tongue curled back, like ट. Many speakers say it as an ordinary n. It never starts a word.

title: क्ष is “ksh”
body: क्ष looks like a single letter but is क + ष, said “ksh”.

title: ग़ is a gargled “gh”
body: ग with a dot below (ग़) is a soft gargling sound at the back of the throat, close to a French “r”. Many speakers say it as ग.

title: ऋ and ृ are said “ri”
body: ऋ and the small hook ृ under a consonant appear in words from Sanskrit. In Hindi they are said “ri”, as in “rip”.

title: ज्ञ is said “gy”
body: ज्ञ is written ज + ञ, but in Hindi it is said “gy”, as in “big yard” said quickly.

title: ः is a light “h” after the vowel
body: The two dots ः (visarga) occur in a few formal words from Sanskrit. Say a light “h” after the vowel; in some words it is hardly heard.
